sm: Albert Mohler opens by discussing President Trump's Friday interview with Ross Douthat on Sixty Minutes, which followed the Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. He says the political content was familiar, but the interview turned theological at the end, with questions about death, the survived assassination attempts, and what comes after. Asked where he goes when he dies, Trump said that as a religious person, in theory he goes to heaven, and that he hopes so because he doesn't want to go to hell. Mohler says this shows little acquaintance with the gospel, and he links Trump's outlook to the prosperity theology of Norman Vincent Peale and Marble Collegiate Church. He also notes Douthat's reference to remarks at Charlie Kirk's memorial service about forgiving enemies.

Douthat asked whether Trump could forgive enemies like James Comey and Nancy Pelosi if that were all it took to enter paradise. Trump said an easy yes would not be real, called them very bad people, and said plainly that he does hate some of his enemies and probably cannot forgive them. Mohler calls it a brave and revealing question, reminds Christians that forgiveness is impossible without God's grace, and says he is praying for the president with renewed urgency. He then previews coverage of the midterms, saying Democratic gains are the biggest reversal since Harry Truman, with Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska still undecided. He begins turning to Israel's inconclusive election, where the president gave Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.

Mohler explains that Eisenkot has twenty-eight days, with a possible extension, to build a coalition, and that if he fails the president will likely turn to Prime Minister Netanyahu. Both men ruled out certain partners, and some parties refuse to work with either, so Mohler expects political uncertainty, though not a collapse of government. He contrasts this with the American system and expresses thanks for the Constitution. He then turns to Governor Gavin Newsom's commutation of the death sentences of all five hundred forty-eight prisoners on California's death row, the largest such mass commutation in modern American history. He notes the governor's power covers only those with a single felony conviction, so many cases may need court or prison review, case by case.

Mohler says the death penalty is grounded in God's covenant with Noah in Genesis chapter nine, affirming the dignity of human life. He notes that California has not executed anyone in a long time, but says the timing of Newsom's move suits a likely 2028 Democratic presidential run. He compares it to President Biden's commutation of thirty-seven of forty federal death sentences, leaving the Tree of Life, Charleston, and Boston Marathon killers, and calls that arbitrary rather than principled. He cites California prosecutors vowing to keep seeking death sentences, noting the governor cannot remove the penalty from the books. One prosecutor warned that without it, prisoners who kill in prison get as many free murders as they wish.
